question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+y\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)\,i+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j$ for $t\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+y\,dy & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$
